lines.text: From clay tablets to bestseller lists, these are the books nearly everyone has heard of. Follow four thousand years of stories that the world could not stop telling.
It begins in ancient Mesopotamia, where a grieving king named Gilgamesh goes looking for eternal life. Pressed into clay, it is one of the oldest stories we have.
In Greece, the poems credited to Homer took shape. The Iliad sings of the rage of Achilles in the last year of the Trojan War.
Its companion, the Odyssey, follows Odysseus on his long voyage home, past monsters and storms. Writers have borrowed his journey ever since.
Around the same time, Greeks were telling Aesop's little animal stories, like the tortoise and the hare, each with a lesson tucked inside.
Far to the east, The Art of War, credited to Sun Tzu, taught that the finest victory is the one you win without a fight.
Over centuries, tales from the Middle East and South Asia gathered around Scheherazade, who tells a new story every night to stay alive. Sinbad sails among them.
Around the year one thousand, the noblewoman Murasaki Shikibu wrote of Prince Genji and the Japanese court. Many call it the first novel.
In Italy, Dante walked through Hell, Purgatory and Paradise in verse. Writing in Tuscan, he helped make it the language of Italy.
In England, Chaucer gathered pilgrims on the road to Canterbury and let each tell a tale, a lively portrait of medieval life left unfinished at his death.
China gave the world Journey to the West, where a monk travels to India for scriptures, guarded by the mischievous Monkey King.
Then came Shakespeare. Romeo and Juliet, two young lovers from feuding families, are still performed and filmed more than four centuries later.
A few years on, a Danish prince wrestled with revenge and asked whether to be, or not to be. Hamlet became one of the most performed plays ever.
In Spain, Cervantes sent a gentleman who had read too many tales of chivalry out to be a knight. Don Quixote is often called the first modern novel.
John Bunyan, writing partly in prison, sent his hero Christian toward the Celestial City. For generations it was the most read English book after the Bible.
In the eighteenth century the novel found its feet. Defoe stranded Robinson Crusoe on a lonely island and started a whole tradition of survival stories.
Jonathan Swift sent Gulliver to lands of tiny people, giants and talking horses, and quietly mocked the politics of his own day.
In China, Dream of the Red Chamber traced the rise and fall of a great noble family, passed around by hand for years before it was finally printed.
In Germany, Goethe told of a scholar who strikes a bargain with the devil. Faust took him a lifetime to finish.
The brothers Grimm gathered the folk tales of their land, Hansel and Gretel and Cinderella among them, and the stories travelled the world.
In England, Jane Austen matched sharp Elizabeth Bennet against proud Mr Darcy. Two centuries later, Pride and Prejudice has never gone out of print.
Just a few years later, a teenage Mary Shelley imagined a scientist who builds a living creature and abandons it. Frankenstein is often called the first science fiction novel.
Charles Dickens sent three ghosts to visit the miser Scrooge one Christmas Eve, and helped shape how Christmas is still celebrated.
In France, Alexandre Dumas gave us d'Artagnan and his three swordsmen friends, all for one and one for all.
That same year Dumas told of a man wrongly imprisoned who escapes, finds a fortune and takes his long revenge.
Charlotte Bronte, writing under a man's pen name, told of an orphan governess who falls for Mr Rochester. Jane Eyre was an instant success.
In the very same year her sister Emily published her only novel, Wuthering Heights, a wild love story out on the Yorkshire moors.
Across the Atlantic, Herman Melville followed Captain Ahab's hunt for a white whale. It sold poorly at first, but now ranks among the great American novels.
Harriet Beecher Stowe's Uncle Tom's Cabin sold in huge numbers and turned many readers against slavery, while parts of the South banned it.
In France, Flaubert wrote of a doctor's wife who escapes a dull life through romance and debt. He was put on trial for it, and acquitted.
Dickens returned with A Tale of Two Cities, set in London and Paris during the French Revolution, and one of the best-selling novels of all time.
Victor Hugo followed the ex-convict Jean Valjean through years of hardship in Les Miserables, a vast story that pleads for the poor.
A tale first told to a real girl on a boat trip became Alice's Adventures in Wonderland, a tumble down the rabbit hole into glorious nonsense.
In St Petersburg, Dostoevsky's poor student commits a murder and is eaten up by guilt. Crime and Punishment probes conscience like few books before it.
Jules Verne put Captain Nemo at the helm of the submarine Nautilus, imagining life under the sea long before it was possible.
That same year, Tolstoy finished War and Peace, following Russian families through Napoleon's invasion, private lives woven into history.
Tolstoy then wrote Anna Karenina, about a noblewoman who leaves her husband for an officer, and a landowner searching for meaning.
Dostoevsky's last novel, The Brothers Karamazov, turns a father's murder into a deep struggle over faith, doubt and guilt.
In Italy, a wooden puppet longed to be a real boy, and his nose grew with every lie. Pinocchio is known the world over.
That same year, Robert Louis Stevenson gave us Long John Silver, pirates, and the treasure map with an X marking the spot.
Mark Twain sent Huck Finn down the Mississippi on a raft with Jim, who had escaped slavery. It became a landmark of American writing.
Oscar Wilde imagined a young man who stays beautiful while his hidden portrait grows old and wicked.
Arthur Conan Doyle collected his detective's cases into a book, and Sherlock Holmes of Baker Street became a household name.
Rudyard Kipling wrote of Mowgli, a boy raised by wolves in the Indian jungle.
Bram Stoker told Dracula through letters and diaries, as friends hunt a vampire count newly arrived in England. It shaped every vampire story since.
As a new century began, a cyclone carried Dorothy from Kansas to the land of Oz, a story later made famous on film.
In India, Rabindranath Tagore's poems in Gitanjali made him the first writer from outside Europe to win the Nobel Prize in Literature.
Marcel Proust began In Search of Lost Time, seven volumes of memory and love that make it one of the longest novels ever written.
In the middle of the First World War, Franz Kafka imagined a man who wakes one morning as a giant insect.
James Joyce packed a single day in Dublin into Ulysses, echoing Homer. Its daring style got it banned for years.
In the Roaring Twenties, Scott Fitzgerald wrote of the mysterious Jay Gatsby and his longing for Daisy, a candidate for the great American novel.
Aldous Huxley imagined a future kept content with engineered births, drugs and endless entertainment, in Brave New World.
Margaret Mitchell told the American Civil War through Scarlett O'Hara, in Gone with the Wind.
Tolkien wrote a story for his children about Bilbo Baggins, some dwarves and a dragon named Smaug. The Hobbit opened the door to Middle-earth.
John Steinbeck followed a farming family from the Dust Bowl to California in the Great Depression. It won the Pulitzer, and was burned in some places.
That same year, Agatha Christie stranded ten strangers on an island and picked them off one by one, perhaps the best-selling mystery ever.
During the Second World War, Albert Camus wrote of a man who kills on an Algerian beach and feels nothing at all.
Antoine de Saint-Exupery sent a little prince from planet to planet to meet a pilot in the desert, one of the most translated books on Earth.
As the war ended, George Orwell's Animal Farm showed farm animals overthrowing their master, only to be ruled by pigs, a sharp satire of Stalin's rule.
Anne Frank's diary, kept while hiding from the Nazis in Amsterdam, was published by her father and became a key witness to the Holocaust.
Orwell then imagined a state that watches everyone and rewrites the past. Nineteen Eighty-Four gave us Big Brother.
C. S. Lewis sent four children through a wardrobe into Narnia, frozen under the White Witch until the lion Aslan returns.
J. D. Salinger's Holden Caulfield wandered New York after being thrown out of school, and his blunt voice won a generation of young readers.
E. B. White wrote the gentle tale of Charlotte's Web, where a clever spider saves the life of a pig.
That same year Hemingway told of an old Cuban fisherman and his long battle with a giant marlin.
Ray Bradbury imagined firemen who burn books, and one who starts to read them. Fahrenheit 451 is a warning about censorship.
Tolkien returned to Middle-earth with The Lord of the Rings, as Frodo sets out to destroy a ring of power. It set the pattern for modern fantasy.
The same year, William Golding stranded schoolboys on an island and watched them slide from order into savagery.
In Nigeria, Chinua Achebe wrote of an Igbo leader as missionaries and British rule arrive. Things Fall Apart became one of the most read African novels.
Harper Lee showed a small Alabama town through a young girl's eyes, as her father defends a Black man falsely accused.
Joseph Heller's bomber crew were trapped by a rule that made sanity impossible to prove, and Catch-22 entered the language.
Roald Dahl gave a poor boy named Charlie a golden ticket to Willy Wonka's wonderful and very strange chocolate factory.
Frank Herbert built the desert planet Arrakis, home of a precious spice. Dune mixed politics, religion and ecology into science fiction.
Gabriel Garcia Marquez followed generations of the Buendia family in Macondo, and brought magical realism to readers everywhere.
Eric Carle's very hungry caterpillar ate its way through a week, and through the hands of millions of small children.
Douglas Adams swept a bewildered Englishman into space just before the Earth was demolished, in The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy.
Salman Rushdie told of children born at the very moment of India's independence, in Midnight's Children.
Margaret Atwood imagined a future theocracy that forces women to bear children for its rulers. The Handmaid's Tale has been retold on stage and screen.
In Japan, Haruki Murakami's Norwegian Wood, a story of love and loss among students in Tokyo, made him famous.
That same year, Toni Morrison wrote Beloved, about a woman who escaped slavery and is haunted by her past.
Stephen Hawking explained the Big Bang and black holes to ordinary readers, and A Brief History of Time stayed on bestseller lists for years.
Paulo Coelho sent a shepherd boy from Andalusia to Egypt in search of a dreamed treasure. The Alchemist became a worldwide bestseller.
George R. R. Martin's A Game of Thrones set noble houses fighting for one throne, and later became a hit television series.
Then an orphan learned he was a wizard. J. K. Rowling's Harry Potter books went on to sell hundreds of millions of copies.
Dan Brown's The Da Vinci Code raced through Paris and London after secrets hidden in art, and sparked fierce debate.
The same year, Khaled Hosseini's The Kite Runner told of friendship and guilt in Afghanistan.
From Sweden, Stieg Larsson paired a journalist with the hacker Lisbeth Salander to solve an old disappearance, starting a series that sold in the tens of millions.
In The Book Thief, Death himself tells of a girl in Nazi Germany who steals books and shares them with a Jewish man hiding below.
Stephenie Meyer's Twilight paired a teenager with a vampire and began a series that sold well over a hundred million copies.
Suzanne Collins imagined teenagers forced to fight to the death on television, and The Hunger Games became books and films.
Hilary Mantel took us to the court of Henry the Eighth in Wolf Hall, following Thomas Cromwell's rise. It won the Booker Prize.
Yuval Noah Harari told the whole history of our species in Sapiens, read by tens of millions.
And Michelle Obama's Becoming traced her life from Chicago's South Side to the White House, one of the best-selling memoirs ever.
From clay tablets to paperbacks, these stories outlived their authors, and are still being read tonight.
